The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: How buses became the lifeline of Madras
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: Packed to the point of tipping over, driven rashly, and battered all over, is how one would describe the MTC buses that ply in the city. While buses were in use in Madras since the 1920s, they really took off only after the tram service met its demise in 1953. Since then, they have become an integral feature of the city and a lifeline for millions

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: How bicycles, motorcycles took over the roads of Madras
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: Bicycles first came to Madras sometime in the 1880s, and at the time, they had a modest start, with there even being demands for a separate lane for cyclists. And while cycles were riding onward, two-wheelers of the motor variety, not so quietly, took to the roads. Brands such as Royal Enfield even set up manufacturing units in the region. To this day, two-wheelers number among the most convenient ways for getting around in the city

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: Hauling about the Madras city on trains
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: Madras was the first place in India where trains were introduced. In 1856, Royapuram became the terminus for a line that ran to Walajah Road. On the suburban side, the ball began rolling in the 1900s, and while the network grew, it never quite rivalled those in places such as Mumbai. Then came the MRTS, which never realised its full potential. At present, Metro Rail is the city’s latest attempt to get back on track

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: When yellow-black taxis cruised the roads of Madras
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: In the 1960s and 1970s, yellow taxis were a force to contend with in Madras. While this mode of transport was never as prolific as its contemporaries, it nonetheless had a presence, with the prepaid taxis at the airport being the chief representative. The yellow-black cab was gradually sidelined by services such as taxis on call and aggregator apps. By 2023, it has been reported that only 304 of them still ride around the city

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: The four key roads of Madras that originate from Fort St. George
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: Madras’ traffic movement is by and large planned on a network created by four great roads. Today, we know them as Rajaji Salai, Kamaraj Salai, EVR Periyar Salai, and Anna Salai, and each retaining their distinct identities. However, their focal point to this day remains Fort Saint George

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: Around Madras city in hand-pulled rickshaws
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: Hand-pulled rickshaws arrived in Madras early in the 20th Century from Japan, and quickly became a convenience despite its very apparent issues. These were later banned in 1973. Their role was replaced by the marginally better cycle rickshaw, which received a helping hand from MGR’s 1971 blockbuster Rickshawkaran

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: Aboard the tramway in Madras
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: When Madras’ first tramway took to the streets in the 1870s, it was horse-drawn. A little over two decades later, the city got its electric tramway system going, much before any other city in the country. Up until its demise in April 1953, the Madras Electric Tramways Company Limited was largely plagued by malfunctions, never once managing to turn a profit

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: Jolted about on carts drawn by oxen and horses in Madras
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: When animal-powered transportation was in its heyday in the Madras region, it came in multiple varieties. While businessmen preferred the fast-moving rekla, which were even used for races, the horse-drawn jhutkas, which became the first public transport of Madras, were in use as recent as 1969. At one point, these carts required a licence and were even exempt from taxes, at least the ones drawn by horses and bullocks

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: Masula boats and the fishermen who kept Madras afloat
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: Before the harbour came into being, arriving in Madras by ship meant making the last leg of the journey on masula boats. These boatmen, who were mostly fishermen from the coast along Madras, knew that they were a vital link in keeping the city’s trade alive and made full use of the opportunity. But by the late 1890s, their era had all but come to an end

The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Title: Of the time when people were carried in palanquins in Madras
The_Hindu_Tamil_Nadu.Description: Palanquins, the very word tracing its origins to the Sanskrit paryanka and the Tamil pallakku, were how the high and mighty got around Madras of the 17th and 18th Centuries. Even records of The East India Company contain details of hire charges of palanquin bearers, with rates higher than even hiring horses. Nowadays, this yesteryear means of transport is mainly consigned to museums
